summary: Passing quietly through Galilee, Jesus tells His disciples again that He will be betrayed, killed and raised; they do not understand and are afraid to ask.
key_insight: Luke places this prediction in a moment of applause, “while everyone marveled at all the things which Jesus did.” Jesus chose that hour to say, “Let these words sink down into your ears.” And He adds a new word: He will be betrayed, handed over.
story: They left that region and passed through Galilee. Jesus did not want anyone to know it, for He was teaching His disciples. {Mk}

While everyone was still marveling at all the things Jesus did, He said to His disciples, “Let these words sink down into your ears, for the Son of Man is about to be betrayed into the hands of men.” {Lk} “And they will kill Him, and the third day He will be raised up.” {Mt}
But they did not understand this saying. It was hidden from them so that they did not perceive it, {Lk} and they were afraid to ask Him about it. And they were exceedingly sorrowful. {Mt}
differences: Matthew says this happened while they were staying in Galilee; Mark says they were passing through Galilee and Jesus wanted no one to know it.
Luke sets the saying while everyone marveled at Jesus’ works and adds “Let these words sink down into your ears.” In Luke, Jesus speaks only of being betrayed, not of His death and rising.
Matthew says the disciples were “exceedingly sorrowful”; Mark and Luke say they did not understand and were afraid to ask.

scene.label: Betrayed
scene.text: The Greek word means handed over or delivered up. The New Testament uses it of Judas, of the leaders who handed Jesus to Pilate, of Pilate who handed Him to be crucified, and of the Father, who “delivered Him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

scene.label: Traveling unnoticed
scene.text: For months Jesus had spent much of His time outside Galilee, in the regions of Tyre and Sidon, the Decapolis and Caesarea Philippi. Now He passed back through Galilee quietly, to teach the Twelve without the crowds of earlier days.

scene.label: Into the hands of men
scene.text: In Daniel 7:13–14 the Son of Man receives dominion and glory from God. Jesus uses that title as He speaks of being handed over to men. Glory and rejection stand side by side in one sentence.

witnesses.matthew: Records the full prediction, including the resurrection on the third day, and notes that the disciples were “exceedingly sorrowful.” They grasped enough to grieve, though the other Gospels show they did not yet understand.
witnesses.mark: Explains why Jesus traveled in secret: He was teaching His disciples. Mark’s next scene shows what filled their minds instead: on the road they argued about who would be the greatest (9:33–34).
witnesses.luke: Sets the saying against the crowd’s amazement and stresses that its meaning was hidden from them. Luke says the same after the third prediction (18:34), until the risen Jesus opens their understanding (24:45).

seeing.reveals: Jesus knows exactly what is coming, betrayal, death and rising on the third day, and He speaks of it in the hour of His popularity. As He later told them, He spoke beforehand so that when it came to pass they would believe (John 13:19).
seeing.living: The disciples were afraid to ask Jesus about the hardest thing He said. Bring Him your questions about the cross and suffering instead of keeping a safe silence. Admiring Jesus’ works is easy; He wants His words about the cross to sink in.
seeing.ponder: Is there something Jesus says that you have been afraid to ask Him about?

preaching.big_idea: Amid the applause, Jesus speaks the hardest words: the Son of Man will be handed over.
outline: A crowd amazed at the majesty of God (43)
A word meant to sink in (44)
A meaning hidden and a question unasked (45)
preaching.watch_for: In Mark and Luke the argument about who is greatest follows at once (Mark 9:33–34; Luke 9:46). Jesus speaks of being handed over; the disciples think about rank.
